posts.quote: Peace is a porch, a quiet evening, and nobody asking what's for dinner.
posts.caption: The house emptied out around 6 last night. My husband went to his brother's for the game, and the grandkids went home with full bellies and a bag of leftover cookies. I stood in the kitchen for a minute listening to nothing. The dishwasher humming. A neighbor's sprinkler. Then I took a glass out to the porch and sat in the rocker that squeaks on the left side. Nobody needed me to find anything. Nobody asked what we were eating. The sun went down behind the Millers' oak tree like it does every night, except this time I actually watched it. Dinner was crackers. Perfect.
posts.first: That rocker belonged to my grandmother. It squeaked on her porch too, same exact spot, for as long as I can remember. My husband keeps offering to oil it. I keep telling him no. Some sounds you don't fix. You just let them keep you company.

posts.quote: I made a grocery list, left it on the counter, and came home with nine things that weren't on it. One of them was a fern.
posts.caption: Saturday, 9:40 a.m., I sat down with a pen and made a real list. Milk, eggs, coffee filters, the good bread. Four things. I even put it in order of the aisles, because I am a woman who plans. Then I walked out the door without it. At the store I relied on instinct, which apparently believes we need a candle called Autumn Hearth, two kinds of crackers, and a fern. The fern was on sale. I don't know what that has to do with anything. I got home and the list was right there on the counter, looking at me. We still have no coffee filters.
posts.first: The fern is doing better than I am, for the record. It's on the windowsill getting the good light. I watered it twice already. I have not watered myself once today, unless you count the wine, which I do.

posts.quote: I found my reading glasses. They were on my head. I'd been wearing them to look for them.
posts.caption: Twenty minutes. That's how long the search went on Saturday morning before I figured it out. I checked the couch cushions, the bathroom counter, the junk drawer, the car, and the pocket of the coat I haven't worn since March. I called my sister to complain about it. She asked what I was reading the junk drawer labels with. I didn't have an answer for that. I went to the hall mirror to make a face at myself and there they were, sitting on top of my head like they'd been watching the whole time. I've decided they were.
posts.first: I own six pairs of readers now. One in the car, one by the bed, one in my purse, one in the kitchen, and two I have never seen again. The kitchen pair has a chip in the left lens from when I sat on them. They're still my favorite.

posts.quote: Told my husband I needed space. He cleaned out one drawer. Twenty-six years and that man still thinks small.
posts.first: He was very proud of that drawer. He showed it to me twice. I put my good scarves in it and said thank you, because twenty-six years also teaches you which battles come with a sandwich afterward and which ones don't.

posts.quote: I don't do drama anymore. I barely do Thursdays.
posts.caption: Somebody at church tried to fill me in on a feud last week. Two women, one casserole dish, a disagreement about whose it was. There were sides. There was a group text. I listened politely for about forty seconds and then I realized I didn't need to know how it ended. It's not that I don't care about people. I care a lot. I just don't have the energy for anything that requires a timeline. These days my calendar has three things on it and one of them is a nap. Thursday showed up anyway this week. I let it in, but I didn't offer it anything to drink.
posts.first: I gave up on a book club once because the meetings had a sign-up sheet for snacks. Not because of the snacks. Because of the sign-up sheet. I knew right then I'd become someone who reads alone, and honestly, I read more now.

posts.quote: My idea of meal prep is deciding at noon which takeout I'm ordering at six.
posts.caption: I bought the containers. The good glass ones with the snap lids, a whole set of twelve, because a woman on the internet made it look peaceful. Sunday afternoons, she said. Chop everything, portion it out, feel in control of your week. That was in March. The containers are still in the box in the pantry, and they look very organized in there. What I do instead is think about dinner around lunchtime, narrow it down to Thai or the pizza place by two, and commit by four. That's planning. That's a system. It's just not the system on the box.
posts.first: The Thai place knows my order now. Last week the girl said "the usual?" before I said a word, and I felt seen in a way I wasn't ready for. I tipped extra. I think we both know what this relationship is.

posts.quote: My knees make a noise every time I stand up. I've started treating it like applause.
posts.caption: The first time it happened in public was at my cousin's wedding. I stood up from the table to go dance, and both knees went off like a bowl of cereal. The whole table heard it. My cousin's new husband actually turned around to see what broke. I could have sat back down and pretended nothing happened. Instead I gave a small bow, fixed my dress, and walked to the dance floor like I'd been announced. Nobody said a word. The DJ played Earth, Wind & Fire. I'm taking that as a sign.
posts.first: My husband says his knees sound like a campfire in the morning. Mine are more of a drumroll. We get up off the couch at the same time sometimes and it sounds like a small band warming up. The dog leaves the room every time. Critics, all of them.

posts.quote: Anyone else hear the doorbell and freeze like a deer, even when you ordered the pizza yourself?
posts.caption: Friday night, 7:40. I had placed the order myself, tracked it on my phone like an air traffic controller, and watched the little car icon turn onto my street. Then the doorbell rang and I froze on the couch like someone had called my name in a library. I muted the TV. I held my breath. I was hiding from my own dinner. It took me a full ten seconds to remember I was the one who invited him. I tipped extra, partly out of guilt. He said have a good night. I absolutely did.
posts.first: When I was a kid, my dad would turn off every light in the house if someone knocked after dark and we weren't expecting them. We'd all sit on the floor and whisper. I used to think it was a game. Turns out it was genetic.

posts.quote: Nobody warns you that one day you'll get excited about a new sponge. Tuesday I got excited about a new sponge.
posts.first: It was a two-pack, blue and yellow, the kind with the scrubby side. I opened it the second I got home. My old sponge had been hanging on since the Fourth of July. I didn't throw it out. I demoted it to the garage, where it will live out its days with dignity.

posts.quote: I stopped ironing in 2009. Nobody noticed. I've applied this lesson broadly.
posts.caption: The iron is still in the hall closet. Top shelf, behind the extra light bulbs, with the cord wrapped around it exactly the way I left it all those years ago. I remember the exact shirt. A white button-down for a work luncheon, and halfway through the left sleeve I just stopped and put it on wrinkled. I sat through two hours of chicken salad and a slideshow and not one person mentioned it. That afternoon, I quit three committees. I've stuck with it ever since, very consistently. It's the only thing I've ever been consistent about.
posts.first: My daughter asked last Christmas why I don't own a steamer. I told her I own a dryer and a little patience. Throw the shirt in for ten minutes with a damp washcloth and go sit down for a while. By the time you're ready, the shirt is too, more or less.

posts.quote: My phone says my screen time is up 40 percent this week. That's the most growth I've shown in years.
posts.caption: It shows up every Sunday morning at 9, right when I'm trying to enjoy my coffee. A little report card nobody asked for. This week it came with an arrow pointing up and a number I'm choosing to read as ambition. Five hours a day. Most of it was looking at houses I'll never buy in towns I'll never visit, and one very long video of a man restoring a rusty pocketknife. I learned a lot about pocketknives. I'd call that education. My phone would call it a problem. We've agreed to disagree.
posts.first: There was a stretch on Wednesday when I watched a woman in Maine reorganize her entire pantry into glass jars. Forty-five minutes. I don't even like her pantry. I just couldn't leave until I knew where the lentils ended up. They went on the top shelf, for the record.

posts.quote: I don't lie about my age. I just stopped attending the birthdays.
posts.caption: My sister called last week asking what I wanted to do for my birthday. I told her nothing. She said that's what I said last year. I said yes, and look how well it went. There's a point where birthdays stop being a party and start being a progress report, and I've read enough of those. So now the day comes and goes like any Wednesday. I have a nice dinner, I buy myself something small, and I do not blow out anything. Nobody sings. Nobody counts. The number goes up anyway, I'm told. I just don't see why I have to attend.
posts.first: My husband tried to sneak a cake in last year. I found it in the garage fridge behind the paint cans. I ate a slice standing up in the garage at 10 p.m. and told him it was delicious. We never spoke of it. That's love.
